title: Paul's Unwavering Ministry
english: By these things, casting out law by law through the law. Just as he says about himself in writing to the Romans: 'For I died by law through law'; that is, having been led by the Mosaic writings, he came to know the piety of the gospel. E caused a marvel in Damascus, and all were exclaiming to themselves:    'Come, behold the Tarsian Jew, a zealous student of the ancestral law, a fierce advocate for Jesus, calling Him up and proving from our writings that this is the Savior according to the promise.' Lest the fear not persuade the whole city, might not the whole people be led and turn away from the law? practitioner of the Scripture, and sharp of mind, and the word is rapid, and the method resourceful, and he has possessed much reliability; from which, knowing our writings accurately, he does not seem to wander in ignorance, but has found the truth through testing and judgment. Into this perplexity he cast a great city, a populous people, the first preaching of the brave convert; and then Damascus was more troubled than Jerusalem previously was when Christians were being stoned, when Stephen Paul was stoning. 8.25.5 Just as the wonderful ones of the best men, wherever they are transferred, carry the victory there, so that lawgiver man always made those people great by the momentum he provided.

having proclaimed the gospel in Phoenicia and having cast the first seeds of the apostolate there, where he himself was also enlightened by knowledge, he came to Jerusalem, a stranger to those there and a fine spectacle. For those who had sent him forward and given the bonds to carry against Christians, not knowing what was happening in the midst, first saw him pleasantly and were eager for the hunt, a multitude of Christian prisoners, hoping to see and seeking the work of the many promises. E word was going forth, I found Paul joining Saul, agreeing in    his conviction and being a more fervent disciple of Christ and of the other apostles; at first they considered the things said to be childishness and mockery, but having tested him, they found him confessing the conviction with his voice, and they deliberated only on one thing: that the young man should be released, as it was not fitting for the Hebrew religion.
And to serve the living Paul and his speaking. And later time clearly showed this.

For even among the many, although they were already Christians, they were not sufficient to live purely according to the gospel, but were wavering and sometimes even coloring [their faith] with circumcision, in order that they might appease the wrath of the Hebrews by partially performing what was granted to them; but this man alone, without yielding anything by an unshakeable mindset, taught, but with a pure voice he proclaimed the word without derivation and progressed so far into the freedom of mindset, that once, regarding the Galatians' domestic dullness and the scarcity of those teaching, he wrote a letter to them against the wonderful life of retreating into the law (cf. Galatians 6:12), by which he taught them to worship and practice religion in the novelty of the citizenship according to Christ, no longer paying attention to the writings from the stone tablets.

He remained bound to what was said of him as the foremost of the apostles and was being purified everywhere, and he fought against Peter, as if Peter were attacking the new citizenship by the use of the old and ceased dogmas; and he neither loved the proximity of the elder nor the prestige of the apostleship when he saw the truth in danger. But he stood up fiercely for the Galatians, and he struck the other many times, as he was, having won the opportunity through boldness.

And everywhere he continued speaking and persuading; and if perhaps he encountered evil men and suffered something terrible, or lived in prison, or received lashes, or was thrown with stones, he did not abandon his readiness because of the occurring failure; but after a short interval, he approached the enemies again, and conversing with the same people, and discovering many ways of undertaking, and being very well-adapted to the falling needs, he went on persuading either all or the many.

And often, indeed, having been found after incurable wounds and having been cast out in the outskirts of that city which he was initiating into piety, and being thought dead because of the greatness of the terrors, having seized the next day's market and having stretched out his right hand, he again taught those who were approaching death; thus, nothing cared for his body, but looking toward the goal of the higher calling (cf. Philippians 3:14), he was patient.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Apostle's Peripatetic Ministry and the Corruption of Priests
english: He was contending from place to place, city from city, enduring earthly labors, facing the dangers from the sea, speaking wisely to inflammatory crowds, and defending himself before angry judges. He was leading the Hebrews into the knowledge of Christ through the Scriptures honored among them, and shaming the Greeks with external words and the unwritten laws of nature; he was confirming Christians, building up converts, and nourishing them with appropriate instruction, just as gardeners tend the young plants with the measured and accustomed flow of waters. Let us learn what most clearly demonstrates his strength in words.

Athens is a city presiding over Achaia, a hearth of words, as those who speak well of it have said, and an ancient workshop of wise men and of those living in words. Since therefore Paul, having run through Illyricum and scattered the sparks of faith everywhere—which, having received from the Spirit, he kept unquenchable—he came according to the necessity of the period to the wise Athenians. And it was a matter worthy of much concern, how the tentmaker might discourse the words concerning God to those who are worthy of ruling all men together according to education.

But, being uplifted by greatness of nature and the wealth of the heavenly gift, he did not take hold of one of the sheltered buildings, nor, sitting at one workshop, did he perform a dialogue, as the first of the philosophers among them were accustomed to do with those approaching; rather, running up to the Areopagus, where there was a harsh and fearful council judging with deadly trials, he found a great multitude gathered there, and stood there lecturing against the rhetoricians according to their customs, those who contended with them daily.

Taking the beginning from an inscription which was attached to an altar, and from there effectively announcing the unknown God to them and concluding with the whole Word, he abstained so much from arguing like a layman about external wisdom, that he converted Dionysius, the most prominent of the Areopagites, along with his wife, and made slaves for Christ, turning many from one altar and one small inscription into many altars.
Descending...

From there, where the warring demon of the Greeks had most power, he moved to the neighboring city, Corinth, the metropolis of Achaia. Speaking in the synagogues, he drove away the salvation-teaching, not just one of the many or those succeeding, but the chief synagogue leader along with his whole household. Having conquered the law from its peak and exalted the cross as a high trophy, he left that city having bowed to Christ.

As time passed and the word of piety was obstructed, he acted like a general, daily seizing cities, villages, and fields, cutting the sinews of the former tyrant. He moved from Corinth to the land of the Pisidians, then seized Lycaonia and the cities of Phrygia, and having visited Asia from there, then Macedonia. He was a common teacher of the inhabited world, benefiting those seeing him by his tongue, and those far away by letters. Only his knee did not tire from traveling, nor his tongue failing, as he unceasingly explained the mysteries of the gospel to enemies and friends.

But such was his teaching; what of the other philosophy of life? He who always persevered in the word and served the gospel, not even taking bread he consumed for free from anyone, but having the struggle against myriads of enemies by day, and by night the toil and the labor of his craft, so that he might have sustenance there, yet appears to all as an apostle driven forth, an unwearied herald, even sparing the bread of those he was hosting.

Let us hear these words, priests, you who do not merely share in the altars, but enrich yourselves from them and feast, making the sacred property your own private possession, and commanding the subordinates like slaves for the sake of Christ. Priesthood is not lordship, but rather for the one who understands, a service; it is not a claim of princely insolence, but an economy of pious ministry. Did not the law-giving Paul not have the authority to eat and drink from the sacred things, and even a little so...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Ministry of John and the Impact of the Word
english: Should he receive the reward of countless labors for the healing of a body being struck daily? But he did not use the authority so that, having taken nothing upon the earth, he might demand all things in the heavens. Therefore, he was even permitted to be superior to man, yet remaining bound to corruptible flesh.

he might also see the earnest of the coming good things and the honors there, he is carried up even unto the third heaven; he sees visions surpassing the lot of those here, and hears unspeakable words, as he himself says (as he himself says in 2 Corinthians 12:2), and while measuring these, he distributes everywhere the greatness and the boasting of one's own advantages. But so that he might only send down the understandings of those growing by small gifts, by necessity a few of his own are stripped bare, and these, having been placed upon another person, he leads far away from the suspicion concerning him.

Thespian, indeed, since in an idea he was carried up to the height by a chariot of fire (as it is written in 1 Kings 18:12), is sung of everywhere and left much wonder by his life; but as far as he reached, no word has interpreted. For, by chance and being raised only a little from the earth by the driving power, he was given to the place where he had the lot to dwell. But the translation of Paul was found more brilliant and glorious, fitting the measure to which he was carried. For he reached as far as the singing of the seven heavens, though a little was lacking for the half-way point.

he Hebrews cast down the understanding against Moses (as it is written in Exodus 19:20), thinking greatly that he alone reached to the summit of Sinai and entered within the ridge and the clouds. For my Paul, instead of a mountain, ascended toward the heavens, and instead of a cloud, wandered beyond the air which is above the cloud. And most fittingly. For it was necessary for the man according to Christ to conquer Moses so much that the Gospel surpasses the Law.

theophanies and the things spoken by God, and how, being bound, he was loosed and, being dejected, was strengthened, and even a dream was his, God making use of him—what is there to say, when he himself did not hide his own grace, but clearly revealed it to all together, saying: 'Do you indeed seek the Christ speaking in me?' For the others, whether prophets or apostles, had timely and chronological activities from above, and at times with them...
It was the divine, and at times it was not present.

This lawgiver was, just as a special temple of God having been completed for Him for habitation, always possessed Christ as a finder of counsel, a teacher of the word, and a partner in all things. And John, the son of Zebedee, seemed great, because among the other disciples he rested boldly upon the Lord's breast (John 13:23); and because of this, he is especially unsung among all.

But this one—how could he not be justly thought to be even above men, he who daily rested not the Jesus in the body, but the Word naked of flesh (John 1:14), having established himself as a very useful and pure vessel for the Creator? And having many and various things to say, as this lawgiver said and did all things, educating the whole world upon earth and sea, in courts, in marketplaces, among the people, and in the courts of kings, intentionally surpassing the multitude.

For I did not set before myself to write a biography of what he achieved, so that nothing might be lacking, but to work a reputation, and this as far as my power reaches. But mentioning only one of the last, I will rest the word.

For since, having circled the whole inhabited world and having placed the great word upon the lamp, he lit the fire of evangelical knowledge, he arrived also at the Romans, as a ruling city, in order to, having initiated and persuaded those holding sway over all men, and having acquired disciples from the surrounding area, speak to the other men. And finding Peter there also, a fellow worker of the same zeal, and having joined a certain holy and inspired company, he educated those under the law in synagogues, and attended to the Gentiles in marketplaces; and he was a diverse teacher of good things, manifesting the pure and unblemished knowledge of God, establishing precise canons of moral virtue, driving away from men debauchery and drunkenness and all unrestrained sensuality, by which especially both the multitude and the one reigning then were held.

Thus, the introduction of the best and most temperate way gripped Nero severely; and he suffered more pain from the destruction of pleasure than if he were being cast out from his own kingship. For he was, if anyone else, a sophist of pleasures.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.
